target: AG1’s claim that animal dissection is largely a productive use of already-deceased animals and therefore does not materially add harm.
objection: Animal dissection is not ethically harmless because the animals used are commonly obtained through inhumane sourcing, including wild capture that harms biodiversity and local populations, so it still causes real animal and environmental harm.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection is educationally necessary or uniquely valuable compared with alternatives.
objection: Synthetic models and computer simulations can teach anatomy and biology equally well or better, so the educational goals of dissection can be met without using real animals.

target: AG1’s implicit assumption that dissection is required by educational or medical training standards.
objection: Dissection is not required by AP Biology or NGSS, and U.S. or Canadian medical schools do not use animals for physician training, so it is not necessary for the relevant curricula or training pathways.

target: AG2’s claim that dissection materially contributes to wild-animal biodiversity loss through wild capture.
objection: The claim that dissection depends on wild-caught animals is unsupported because over 98% of dissection animals were already deceased and fetal pigs are meat-industry byproducts, so dissection specimens are not primarily obtained through wild capture.

target: AG2’s claim that synthetic models and computer simulations can fully replace real dissection without loss of educational value.
objection: Synthetic models and computer simulations should not be presumed to provide the same fine-motor, hand-eye coordination, and critical-thinking benefits as handling real specimens in dissection.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection animals are mostly already-deceased byproducts and thus ethically unproblematic.
objection: Even if animals are described as already deceased or as byproducts, obtaining them still depends on upstream animal killing or production processes, so dissection is not ethically harmless.

target: AG1’s claim that alternatives can be treated as equivalent to real dissection.
objection: Synthetic models and computer simulations let students learn anatomy without using animal bodies at all, so animal dissection is avoidable in education.

target: AG2’s claim that simulations can match dissection’s critical-thinking benefits.
objection: There is no evidence that simulations produce the same critical-thinking learning outcomes as real dissection, so alternatives cannot simply be assumed equivalent.

target: AG1’s assumption that there is no evidence alternatives can match dissection’s critical-thinking outcomes.
objection: Simulation-based anatomy instruction can support the same critical-thinking processes because students can examine and analyze anatomical structures in 3D models and simulations, and there is evidence that such alternatives can match or exceed dissection outcomes.

target: AG2’s claim that simulation alternatives can replace dissection’s skill and motivation benefits.
objection: Synthetic models and computer simulations cannot be presumed to deliver the same combined fine-motor, hand-eye coordination, and ‘aha moment’ motivation benefits as real specimen dissection.

target: AG1’s claim that simulations can match fine-motor and hand-eye coordination benefits.
objection: Interactive manipulation in simulations and synthetic models can train hand-eye coordination and fine-motor control in ways similar to practical specimen work, so there is evidence alternatives can provide comparable psychomotor benefits.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection is justified because curricular standards do not explicitly forbid it.
objection: The fact that AP Biology or NGSS do not require dissection does not itself justify keeping it, because standards set learning expectations rather than endorsing any teaching method that is not forbidden.

target: AG1’s claim that animal dissection is ethically acceptable if it has educational value.
objection: Educational practices should not require inhumane harm to animals or environmentally harmful outcomes, so the educational value of dissection does not by itself justify it.

target: AG2’s claim that dissection is ethically harmful because it requires obtaining animal bodies for specimens.
objection: Typical classroom dissection repurposes already-deceased meat-industry byproducts rather than requiring new killing or capture, so it does not necessarily impose the additional harm the objection assumes.

target: AG2’s claim that dissection should be rejected on ethics grounds because it requires harm.
objection: A classroom practice should be allowed when it meaningfully improves learning and does not materially increase harm; dissection provides educational benefits and can use already-deceased byproducts, so it should not be categorically banned.

target: AG1’s claim that byproduct-based sourcing means dissection does not require harmful animal sourcing.
objection: Evidence that approximately 99% of dissection animals are caught in the wild shows that specimens are commonly obtained through new inhumane capture, not merely byproduct disposal.
